new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work is listed for this item and the reader opened and quoted it, so there were no silent or not-opened works to spot-check. As a substitute I scanned every 'stress'/'accent' hit in the full thesis text (PDF pp. 90, 173, 194, 195, 254, 255, 354, 382). The only stress mention not in the report is p.72 (PDF 90): the indefinite article be is 'phonologically independent, carrying its own pitch/stress', whereas the bound clitic -be 'does not carry any independent pitch/stress'; p.237 (PDF 255) adds 'despite the loss of stress, the construction is productive'. Both are consistent with the report and add nothing about stress placement. p.155 ('Longacre stresses that') is the verb; p.364 i…

sources.note: BARAI (Birari dialect, upper Bariji; note 1 p.511), not Namiae. p.474: 'Stress is contrastive on the word level and is defined as a combination of pitch, and either length or intensity. There are two contrastive pitch levels, high and low. To mark stress, high pitch combines with increased intensity and low pitch combines with length. Note the four possible combinations on the following two syllable words: íko before, ikò sew, ìre food, and iré stand.' 'Secondary stress has been observed in the longer words but needs further analysis.'

sources.note: pp.69-70: Kokora (Upper Bariji) listed as the most divergent of nine Barai dialects -- no phonology for it. Sect 5.82.6 p.135: stress interpretation in Koita, Mountain Koiari and Barai 'needs further investigation'. Sect 5.83.63 p.144 (his Barai = southern Pitoni dialect): 'Insufficient time was spent on this aspect of the language to determine the status of stress in it. My impression is, however, that stress is probably phonemic since primary stress has variant positions in words of the same number of syllables, e.g., [moʔga] 'tanket (shrub)'; [ʔmisu] 'salt'.'
